content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper analyzes SGD with the goal of showing high probability convergence bounds. Standard analyzes involves bounding a martingale with variance process $\|x_t-x^\star\|^2$. When the domain is bounded, this variance is also bounded and so standard concentration results yield $\tilde O(1/\sqrt{T})$ convergence rates in high probability.

In this work, the authors essentially show that $\|x_t-x^\star\|^2$ is anyway bounded by roughly $O(\|x_1-x_\star\|^2)$ and so the relevant martingale will still concentrate. This boundedness is established by first showing that the sum of the distances is bounded by a this martingale whose variance process is the distances. Then, some natural concentration arguments show that this martingale is bounded in high probability by a function of the sum of the distances, which leads to a kind of implicit equation that  can be rearranged to obtain a bound on the distances.

Extensions are presented to smooth losses and last iterate convergence.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The results are new to my knowledge and the analysis is reasonably straightforward. The notion that the iterates are bounded without extra projections has recently been explored in a other works (e.g. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.10785.pdf,  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.06915.pdf, and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.02160.pdf, which should probably be mentioned). Although these have slightly more specialized settings, it is unsurprising that similar results hold for SGD with constant learning rate. In fact, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.10785.pdf seems especially relevant for the related work discussion: although the results require clipping, this can easily be omitted in the case of light tailed gradient estimates considered in this paper.


I think the results would be improved quite a bit by also not requiring bounded gradient noise. Is there any actual difficulty in moving to at least subgaussian noise? The bounded (and even subgaussian) model is especially weird when considering the smooth but not Lipschitz setting: notice that the motivating example for smooth losses (linear regression) will likely not satisfy the assumptions. A more natural noise model might involve noise bounded in terms of the actual gradient value or the distance to opt.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Note that the last-iterate guarantee in expectation for unbounded domains (but not in high probability) can be found in the following blog post: https://parameterfree.com/2020/08/07/last-iterate-of-sgd-converges-even-in-unbounded-domains/, and possibly elsewhere as well.

So I would not say that it is not known in expectation.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper introduces a nice analysis of high probability bounds. The techniques are not too complicated and the results close a gap in the literature.

The major negative is that perhaps the gap being closed is not too large. IMO the most important part of the paper is likely the “by-product” bound on the individual iterates.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes high-probability analysis of SGD under almost surely bounded noise assumption for convex Lipschitz/smooth problems. Unlike many existing works, this paper does not rely on the assumption that the domain is bounded. The authors also formulate the result for the final iterate of SGD and prove high-probability results for SGD with momentum.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
1. **Clarity.** I like the way the paper is written: the problem is well-motivated, the setup and results are also presented well. The authors explain well what is the key challenge arising in the high-probability analysis of SGD.

2. **Arbitrary closed convex domain.** Not many works on high-probability analysis of stochastic methods allow such generality in the choice of the domain (in fact, I am aware only of [1]).

## Weaknesses

1. **Almost surely bounded noise assumption.** The analysis relies on almost surely bounded noise assumption (Assumption 3.1). This is a very restrictive assumption and even when it holds, the upper bound on the noise norm $M$ can be very large. Moreover, there exist works that also do not rely on the bounded domain assumption but rely on a much more general assumption of the bounded variance, see [1] and [2,3] (though these papers consider not exactly SGD and the latter two works consider unconstrained problems only). I believe that the analysis presented in the paper should be extended at least to the case of sub-Gaussian noise like in the classical works on high-probability analysis (see [4]). Without this, the study is incomplete and below the standards established in the literature on high-probability analysis of stochastic methods.

2. **Positioning in the literature requires improvements. Important related works are not discussed.** The authors sometimes refer to different methods as SGD. For example, in the second paragraph from Section 2, the second sentence says: "The high probability error bounds of SGD is scarce in early works but have received substantial attention in recent years (Kakade & Tewari, 2008; Rakhlin et al., 2012; Hazan & Kale, 2014; Harvey et al., 2019; Feldman & Vondr´ak, 2019; Li & Orabona, 2020; Jain et al., 2021; Varre et al., 2021; Cutkosky & Mehta, 2021; Liu & Lu, 2021; Davis et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2022)." Some of the works mentioned there focus on different stochastic methods, e.g., (Cutkosky & Mehta, 2021; Davis et al., 2021). In some other sentences (e.g., the second sentence of the abstract), the authors claim that the existing works rely on the bounded domain assumption. However, this is not true: for example, [1,2,3] do not make such assumption, though consider different algorithms. In particular, the results of this work are weaker than the ones from [3], who also consider convex smooth and non-smooth problems, but analyze their methods under more general assumptions.

Moreover, the idea of proving that the iterates produced by a stochastic method stay in the bounded region with high-probability to apply Freedman's type inequalities is not new: for example, it was used in papers [2, 3], though the mentioned works consider only unconstrained problems and methods with clipping. Nevertheless, the authors should improve the positioning of their work in the literature and discuss [1, 2, 3] in more details. If the authors are focusing only on SGD, it makes sense, but then all claims should be modified accordingly + in view of the first weakness, the assumption on the noise should be generalized.

3. **No proof for the last-iterate convergence result for SGD.** I find the result stated in Corollary 7.2 to be very interesting. Unfortunately, the authors do not provide the proof of this result.

4. **Motivation of the analysis of the momentum version.** The analysis of SGD with momentum is presented, but the authors do not provide the motivation/discussion of this result. In particular, what is the theoretical value of this given the fact that the derived rate is the same as for SGD? There exist other momentum versions of SGD that give much more -- accelerated high-probability convergence results, see [1, 2, 3].

---
References

[1] Damek Davis, Dmitriy Drusvyatskiy, Lin Xiao, and Junyu Zhang. From low probability to high confidence in stochastic convex optimization. J. Mach. Learn. Res., 22:49:1–49:38, 2021.

[2] Gorbunov, Eduard, Marina Danilova, and Alexander Gasnikov. "Stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed noise via accelerated gradient clipping." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (2020): 15042-15053.

[3] Gorbunov, Eduard, Marina Danilova, Innokentiy Shibaev, Pavel Dvurechensky, and Alexander Gasnikov. "Near-optimal high probability complexity bounds for non-smooth stochastic optimization with heavy-tailed noise." arXiv preprint arXiv:2106.05958 (2021).

[4] Ghadimi, Saeed, and Guanghui Lan. "Optimal stochastic approximation algorithms for strongly convex stochastic composite optimization i: A generic algorithmic framework." SIAM Journal on Optimization 22, no. 4 (2012): 1469-1492.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly-written and the proofs seem to be correct. Formally the results are novel, though the techniques and ideas are already presented in the literature.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the weaknesses outweigh the strengths and I believe that the paper requires several improvements and more accurate positioning in the literature on high-probability analysis of stochastic methods. Unfortunately, in the current shape, I have to recommend the rejection. If the authors modify the paper according to the issues I raised, the paper will change significantly and thus will require another full round of review (so, in this case, one also cannot accept the paper to ICLR 2023). Nevertheless, I encourage the authors to apply all necessary corrections and resubmit to the next big conference or to a journal.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an analysis of optimization of a convex function via projected stochastic gradient descent. The noise insterted at each SGD step is assumed to be mean-0 and bounded, and the function is assumed to be either Lipschitz or convex. In both cases, high-probability bound is shown on the averaged and last-iterate values of the solution after $T$ steps. The main term in that bound is $O(\log(1/\delta)/\sqrt{T})$ where $1-\delta$ is the desired probability of success. A key point of this bound is that it does not require the domain to be bounded. Extensions and related results are also presented.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*Strengths*

- It is nice to have a result like the one proven here even when the domain is bounded, as bounds involving diameter bounds can be pessimistic. 

*Weaknesses*

- Readers knowledgeable about SGD will recognize that the main proof elements (including the version of Freedman's inequality) come from Harvey et al. I will say more about this below. 
- The assumption of bounded noise is quite limiting in practice. I would expect that, the further away a point is from the global minimizer, the larger the norm of the noise might be (linear regression is a case in point). Notice that this may be true even when the randomness in the problem is "light tailed". 
- The effect of term $M$ appearing in the concentration bounds might be ameliorated somewhat. If one makes the assumption that the covariance of the noise is bounded by a multiple of the identity (say), then $M$ may be replaced by this constant, although a "Bernstein-type" extra factor will appear in the concentration bounds.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is quite clear and is (seemingly) correct, but I think its contribution is fairly incremental, not too original, and still too restrictive to be of practical use. 

1) The proofs basically reproduce the argument Harvey et al (using the same concentration inequality), while noting that it also gives bounds on the distance between iterates and the global minimum. This last fact is a slight extension of well-known "Féjer monotonicity" from standard optimization, and its proof is neither hard, nor surprising. Some light adaptations are needed to consider the smooth case, but those only require standard results from basic first-order optimization.

2) The issue of unbounded feasible sets has been considered in the setting of variational inequalities, see eg. https://doi.org/10.1137/15M1031953. Other papers have taken up on the same idea. 

3) As I mentioned above, the $M$ term has too big an effect on the concentration bounds. In practice one would expect this to depend heavily on the dimension of the problem.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper makes a modest contribution to the analysis of SGD over (unbounded) feasible sets. The main techniques and ideas come from previous work, and the result itselt is not particularly surprising nor very useful.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper shows some high probability analysis of SGD algorithm in convex setting, with the advantage that the analysis does not require the bounded domain assumption.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper provides a nice analysis for SGD in convex setting where the iterates are not required to stay in a bounded region. However, most of the results are based on the framework from Harvey et al. (2019), thus the improvement is not particularly interesting. In addition, while the authors did not assume the bounded region, they assume that the gradient noise is bounded, which restricted the setting. 

Since this paper claims to remove the bounded domain assumption, I find it confusing when the authors state the projected version of SGD. If the iterates are bounded (with high probability), why we still need to consider the projection step?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The novelty is not much because the theoretical framework is similar to Harvey et al. (2019).

Comments on clarity:
- The abstract is confusing since it mention $\delta$ without any definition. 
- Typo/Grammar in page 3 'it is challenge to' -> 'it is challenging to'
content.summary_of_the_review: Although this paper presents some nice results for SGD with high probability, they are not major contributions since the analysis for convex SGD has been analyzed thoroughly in literature. The novelty is limited since the proofs rely from the framework of the reference Harvey et al. (2019), which also devoted to analyze SGD in convex setting.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
